title: Shakalya's last question
hook: the last challenger argues to win, the warning that stopped Gargi comes true for him, and a riddle about a tree ends the debate
carry: the root of a person is knowing and joy
tomorrow: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shakalya's countdown, from 3,306 gods all the way to one. Your line was truth is one; the wise call it many names.
screen: `TRUTH IS ONE; THE WISE CALL IT MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: After the countdown, Shakalya doesn't sit down. He keeps firing questions: the gods of each direction, what the heart rests on, what the self is founded on. Yajnavalkya answers each one. Then, somewhere in the middle, he stops and asks Shakalya something. Shakalya, have these scholars made you their coal-tongs? Their tool for pulling hot coals out of the fire, so they don't burn their own hands?
screen: `HE DOESN'T SIT DOWN.` → `QUESTION AFTER QUESTION.` → `HAVE THEY MADE YOU THEIR COAL-TONGS?`

segments.voice: That line tells you what's going on. Shakalya isn't Gargi, chasing a question to its edge. The others have sent him in to do the burning work for them, to win. And he keeps going. So at last Yajnavalkya turns the debate around. Now I ask you, he says, about the person taught in the Upanishads. If you can't tell me who he is, your head will fall off. Shakalya didn't know. And his head fell off: the text tells it in one plain sentence. Some readers take it literally, as the real stake of these Vedic debates; others hear an image: his whole argument came apart. Either way, set it beside Gargi. She got the same warning, stopped, and came back with better questions. Then Yajnavalkya asks the room one last riddle. A person is like a tree: hair for leaves, skin for bark, bones for the wood inside. Cut a tree down, and it grows again from the root. When death cuts a person down, from what root does he grow? Nobody in the room dares take him on. The chapter closes on its answer: Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy. That's the teaching. Under everything you are, there's a root no argument and no death can cut, and it isn't dull or blank: it is awareness, and it is joy. Later Vedanta teachers gather this into a famous name for Brahman: sat-chit-ananda, being, awareness, joy. Shakalya staked his head on winning. The Upanishad says your root was never in the winning. Lose the argument, lose the job, lose someone you love: you've been cut down, not uprooted.
screen: `SENT IN TO WIN FOR THE OTHERS.` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW, AND HIS HEAD FELL.` · `FROM WHAT ROOT DOES A PERSON GROW?` · `BRAHMAN: KNOWING, AND JOY.` · then, large: `THE ROOT OF A PERSON IS KNOWING AND JOY.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself as a tree: hair like leaves, skin like bark, bones like the hard wood inside, the body's weight settling like roots into soil. Ask the old riddle, from what root do I grow, and let the text's answer rest in the body, not the head: knowing, and joy. If you pray, offer your prayer to that root; if not, simply rest there.
Murdha, the head. Shakalya staked his on winning, and lost it. The root, the text says, was never in the stakes.
Your line: the root of a person is knowing and joy. Gargi asked to know; Shakalya argued to win. Day three hundred eighty-one, done.

howItsDone: The Vedic brahmodya, a formal contest of questions about Brahman, is the setting of this chapter; teachers of the Upanishads read Shakalya's end alongside Gargi's warning, and the closing tree verses end the third book with a riddle.

fork.reveal: vijnanam anandam brahma: Brahman, knowing and joy. later Vedanta calls Brahman sat-chit-ananda: being, awareness, joy.

original.note: Sanskrit mūrdhan (nominative mūrdhā): the head, the top. the stake in the Brihadaranyaka's debates.

Shakalya.meaning: the challenger who kept pushing questions for the others

Gargi.meaning: the woman scholar who got the same warning and stopped

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage who answers the challengers in Janaka's court

Upanishads.meaning: ancient texts on the self and Brahman, the Vedas' last part

Brahman.meaning: the great reality; here, the root, knowing and joy

sat-chit-ananda.meaning: being, awareness, joy: a Vedanta name for Brahman
